title: SHE GAVE HIM THREE SONS… BUT STILL COULDN’T MAKE HIM LOVE HER.
paragraphs: SHE GAVE HIM THREE SONS… BUT STILL COULDN’T MAKE HIM LOVE HER.
Leah’s heartbreaking words in Genesis 29:34 reveal the silent agony of being needed but never chosen—and the astonishing grace of a God who sees the person everyone else overlooks.
She had just given birth to her third son.
Her body had endured another pregnancy. Her arms were holding another miracle. Another child had entered the world.
And somewhere inside her exhausted heart, a desperate hope was rising.
Maybe now.
Maybe this time he would look at her differently.
Maybe this time he would stop comparing her to her sister.
Maybe this time she would finally become more than the woman he had married but never truly wanted.
Then Leah spoke words that have survived thousands of years.
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons.” — Genesis 29:34 (KJV)
Read that again.
She had given birth to three sons, yet her deepest longing was still to be loved by her husband.
She wasn't asking for a palace.
She wasn't asking for riches.
She was asking for something that should never have required three pregnancies to earn.
To be loved.
And perhaps that is why her story hurts so much.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to keep giving, keep sacrificing, keep trying, and still wonder why they are not enough.
You may never have stood in Leah's tent.
But you may have cried Leah's tears.
And what happens next in her story reveals something far greater than the tragedy of an unloved wife.
It reveals the God who sees the rejected—and the grace that eventually leads us to Jesus Christ.
Before we reach that beautiful truth, however, we need to understand the wound Leah was carrying.
Because this story did not begin with a baby.
It began with a deception.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Scripture makes that unmistakably clear.
Genesis 29:18 says, “And Jacob loved Rachel.”
He loved her so much that he agreed to work seven years for her hand in marriage.
Seven years.
Imagine being loved with that kind of anticipation.
Imagine someone looking toward the future and seeing you in it.
Rachel had that kind of affection from Jacob.
Leah did not.
After seven years of labor, Rachel and Leah's father, Laban, deceived Jacob by giving Leah to him in marriage instead of Rachel.
When Jacob discovered the deception, he confronted Laban.
He had worked for Rachel.
But he had been given Leah.
The Bible does not tell us everything Leah knew, wanted, or felt about her father's scheme. We must be careful not to invent what Scripture leaves unsaid.
What it does tell us is devastating enough.
Jacob subsequently married Rachel, and Genesis 29:30 says that he loved Rachel more than Leah.
Imagine living inside that comparison.
Two sisters.
One husband.
One woman receiving the affection the other desperately wanted.
And Leah had to live with that painful reality.
She could not become Rachel.
She could not erase what her father had done.
She could not force Jacob's heart to love her equally.
But she could still hope.
Perhaps a child would change things.
Perhaps motherhood would bring the affection marriage had not.
Then Scripture gives us one of the most tender statements in the Old Testament.
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” — Genesis 29:31 (KJV)
Pause there.
The LORD saw.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה
Vayyar YHWH ki-senu'ah Le'ah.
A close translation is, “And the LORD saw that Leah was hated.”

The Hebrew word שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah) comes from a root meaning “to hate.” In this relational context, Genesis 29:30 helps us understand Leah's condition: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. The language expresses the painful reality of Leah being less loved, even rejected in comparison.
We should not soften her suffering.
But neither should we assume the text tells us Jacob's every private feeling.
The point is clear.
Leah was living in a marriage marked by unequal affection.
And God saw her.
Not because she had finally convinced Jacob to notice her.
Not because she had become more beautiful than Rachel.
Not because she had earned divine attention through suffering.
God saw her because He is the God who sees.
Somebody needs to hear that today.
Being overlooked by someone you love does not mean you have been overlooked by God.
He sees the tears you wipe away before anyone enters the room.
He sees the exhaustion beneath your smile.
He sees the prayers you are almost embarrassed to pray again because you have prayed them so many times.
He sees the quiet heartbreak of being surrounded by people while feeling painfully alone.
But there is something important here.
God's compassion for Leah did not mean every part of her painful situation immediately changed.
And that is where this story becomes uncomfortably real.
Because sometimes God sees us while we are still waiting.
Sometimes His presence does not mean the person who hurt us suddenly becomes the person we hoped they would be.
Sometimes His mercy meets us in a place we would never have chosen.
Leah conceived and gave birth to her first son.
She named him Reuben.
Genesis 29:32 records her explanation:
“Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.”
The name Reuben is associated in the narrative with seeing.
Leah recognized that God had seen her affliction.
But notice where her hope immediately turned.
Now my husband will love me.
She acknowledged God's attention while still desperately longing for Jacob's affection.
And we should not condemn her for wanting her husband's love.
That desire was not sinful.
Marriage was never intended to be a place where one spouse must beg for tenderness.
But Leah's words reveal how deeply her heart had become entangled with a hope she could not control.
Then she gave birth to another son.
Simeon.
Genesis 29:33 says:
“Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also.”
The name Simeon is connected in the narrative with hearing.
First, God saw.
Now, God heard.
And yet Leah's marital sorrow remained.
Then came her third son.
Levi.
And the words that should stop every reader in their tracks:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons.”
In Hebrew, the crucial expression is:
עַתָּה הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי
Attah happa'am yillaveh ishi elai.
“Now this time my husband will be joined to me.”
The verb יִלָּוֶה (yillaveh) carries the sense of being joined or attached, and it forms the wordplay behind the name לֵוִי (Levi).
Leah was not merely celebrating a birth.
She was expressing her longing for attachment.
Connection.
Closeness.
A marriage in which she would no longer feel like the unwanted woman standing beside the beloved one.
And there is something almost unbearable about those words.
“Now this time…”
How many people have lived inside that sentence?
Now this time, if I become more attractive, they will love me.
Now this time, if I earn more money, my family will respect me.
Now this time, if I stop making mistakes, they will accept me.
Now this time, if I serve harder at church, people will notice me.
Now this time, if I forgive them again, perhaps they will finally treat me differently.
Now this time, if I give everything I have left, maybe I will finally be enough.
But there is a painful difference between loving someone faithfully and believing you must continually prove that you deserve love.
Leah was not wrong to want affection.
The tragedy was that she kept hoping another child would accomplish what only a changed human heart could provide.
And here is the question that reaches beyond Leah's marriage.
What have you been trying to produce in order to convince someone that you are worth loving?
An achievement?
A perfect appearance?
A successful career?
A reputation?
A lifetime of pleasing everyone?
A version of yourself that never complains, never struggles, never needs anything?
Perhaps you have become so skilled at making everyone else comfortable that nobody realizes how uncomfortable you have become inside your own life.
You keep saying, “I'm okay.”
But you are tired.
You keep showing up.
But something inside you is quietly breaking.
You keep praying.
But sometimes your prayers are less like polished sentences and more like tears falling onto a pillow.
And underneath all of it is a question you are almost afraid to ask.
Lord, when will I finally be enough?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not answer that question by telling you to become more impressive.
It tells you about a Savior who came to rescue sinners who could never earn salvation through their own performance.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became flawless.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And it changes everything.
Because human love, even at its healthiest, cannot carry the full weight of being our savior.
A spouse cannot forgive our sins before God.
A parent's approval cannot make us righteous.
A thousand compliments cannot resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
Only Jesus Christ can reconcile us to God.
And when we begin demanding from human relationships what only Christ can ultimately give, we place impossible burdens on ourselves and others.
That does not mean we should accept mistreatment.
It does not mean a neglected spouse should simply endure cruelty without seeking help.
It does not mean human affection is unimportant.
It means that our ultimate identity and hope must be anchored in Someone greater than the approval of another person.
Jesus Christ is not merely another voice telling you that you matter. He is the crucified and risen Savior through whom sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
And Leah's story contains another remarkable turn.
After Levi, she conceived again.
Her fourth son was Judah.
This time, Genesis 29:35 records her words:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
The Hebrew reads:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Happa'am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
The name Judah, יְהוּדָה (Yehudah), is associated in this passage with the Hebrew verb for praising or giving thanks.
Do you see the change in her words?
With Reuben, she hoped Jacob would love her.
With Simeon, she spoke of God hearing her rejection.
With Levi, she hoped her husband would become attached to her.
But with Judah, she said:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
For this moment, her recorded words turn away from the question of Jacob's affection and toward praise of God.
We should not claim that Leah's emotional wounds were instantly healed or that she never struggled again. Genesis does not say that, and her later story remains complicated.
But this moment matters.
The woman who had repeatedly spoken about her longing for her husband now spoke directly about praising the LORD.
And here is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
Leah could not have known the full significance of Judah's family line.
Generations later, God's covenant promises would unfold through Judah's descendants.
King David would come from Judah's tribe.
And according to Matthew 1, the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ would trace through Judah.
The fourth son of the woman who had been less loved became an ancestor of the Messiah.
Let that settle in your heart.
The woman who struggled to feel chosen in her own marriage belonged to the family line through which the promised Savior would come.
This does not mean Leah earned that privilege by suffering.
It does not mean Rachel was less valuable to God.
It does not mean every rejected person will receive an extraordinary earthly reward.
It means that God's redemptive purposes are not limited by the rankings, preferences, and prejudices of human beings.
God was working through a deeply broken family.
A family marked by deception.
Favoritism.
Jealousy.
Competition.
And painful relationships.
Yet human sin did not defeat God's covenant faithfulness.
And ultimately, that covenant story leads us to Jesus.
Revelation 5:5 calls Him “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
Consider the wonder of that title.
Judah.
Leah's son.
The son whose name was connected with praise.
From that lineage came the promised Messiah.
The One who would be despised and rejected by men, as Isaiah 53:3 foretold.
The One who would enter a world of broken hearts and sinful people.
The One who would bear our sins upon the cross.
The One who would rise from the dead, defeating sin and death.
And through Him, the greatest scandal of human history—our rebellion against a holy God—would meet the astonishing grace of divine redemption.
This is why the story cannot end with Leah's longing for Jacob.
It must lead us to Christ.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve our self-esteem.
He came to save us from our sins.
Matthew 1:21 says:
“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
And that includes the sins we commit while trying to survive our pain.
The bitterness we secretly nurse.
The jealousy we refuse to confess.
The people we manipulate because we are terrified of losing them.
The pride that makes us desperate to appear important.
The resentment that grows when somebody else receives the affection, opportunity, or recognition we wanted.
Leah's story invites compassion.
But the Gospel also calls every one of us to repentance.
Not because wounded people are responsible for the sins committed against them.
But because every human heart, wounded or not, needs the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps your deepest struggle is not that you have never been loved.
Perhaps it is that you have been searching for ultimate security in a love that was never designed to replace God.
Perhaps you have allowed somebody else's rejection to define your entire existence.
Perhaps you have become so consumed with being chosen by people that you have neglected the Lord who calls you to come to Him.
Jesus says in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
He does not promise that every difficult marriage will be restored.
He does not promise that every person who rejected you will apologize.
He does not promise that obedience will eliminate every painful memory.
But He offers something infinitely greater than a guarantee of human approval.
He offers Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
Rest for the weary soul.
A new life grounded in His grace.
And a hope that death itself cannot destroy.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting beside someone who no longer seems to notice you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make your parents proud.
Maybe you are the child who always felt compared with a more successful sibling.
Maybe you are the friend who remembers everyone's birthday but is forgotten on your own.
Maybe you are the believer who serves quietly while others receive the recognition.
Or maybe you are the person who has been smiling through a heartbreak nobody knows exists.
The story of Leah does not promise that everyone will finally appreciate you.
But it reminds you that God sees what others overlook.
And the Gospel reveals the fullest expression of God's saving love in Jesus Christ.
You do not have to make another person your messiah.
You do not have to pretend your wounds are healed when they are not.
You can bring your grief to God.
You can ask Him for wisdom.
You can seek healthy help and godly counsel.
You can establish necessary boundaries where there is harm.
You can forgive without pretending that evil was good.
And by His grace, you can stop allowing rejection to become the final word over your life.
Because rejection may describe something you experienced.
It does not have the authority to determine who you are before God.
If you belong to Jesus Christ through faith, your identity is rooted in His finished work, not in the shifting opinions of people.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Even your salvation cannot be earned through performance.
How much less should you believe that your eternal worth depends on finally impressing another human being?
And perhaps this is the moment for a different prayer.
Not merely, “Lord, make them love me.”
But:

Lord Jesus, teach me to love You above every human approval. Heal the places where rejection has distorted my identity. Forgive the ways I have sinned while trying to fill the emptiness inside me. Give me courage to face the truth, wisdom to make healthy decisions, and grace to forgive as You have forgiven me. Teach me to rest in Your finished work rather than endlessly trying to prove myself. Amen.
If that prayer reflects the condition of your heart, do not rush past it.
Sometimes the most important moment in reading Scripture is not when we learn something new.
It is when the Word of God exposes something we have been carrying for years.
And perhaps someone else is carrying that same pain tonight.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be giving everything to a relationship while silently believing they are impossible to love.
Someone may be struggling with rejection and wondering whether God sees them at all.
You do not have to explain a private struggle publicly to be worthy of prayer.
Your testimony may encourage someone who thought they were the only one fighting this battle.
And if this message has brought you closer to Scripture, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, teach biblical truth, call hearts to repentance, encourage struggling believers, and point wounded people toward the hope of the Gospel.
But this mission is not sustained by words alone.
It takes time, effort, resources, and the faithful generosity of people who believe that the truth of God's Word should continue reaching others.
And please understand this clearly.
The Gospel is free. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ.
But if God has given you the desire and ability to help spread His Word, financial generosity can be one meaningful expression of worship and partnership in Gospel ministry.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not a pressured giver.
Not a frightened giver.
A cheerful giver.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to encourage others, but the heart of the mission will always be Jesus Christ, not merchandise.
Encourage a struggling believer to read the Scriptures.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Pray for the Gospel to reach people who desperately need the truth.
Because the goal is not merely to grow an audience.
It is to see people encounter the Word of God, repent, believe in Jesus Christ, grow as disciples, and carry the Gospel into the world.
And before you leave, return with me one final time to Leah.
Picture her holding Levi.
Her third son.
A precious child.
A mother with a heart still longing for affection.
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me.”
She could not see the generations ahead.
She could not see David.
She could not see Bethlehem.
She could not see the cross.
She could not see the empty tomb.
And we must remember that Levi was not the ancestor through whom the Messiah's royal line came. That distinction belonged to Judah, her next son.
But God was already working in a family whose brokenness was painfully visible.
Leah wanted her husband to be joined to her.
And through another son she would bear, the family line would eventually lead to the Savior through whom sinners are reconciled to God.
What an astonishing contrast.
One woman's longing for human attachment.
And God's unfolding purpose to bring redemption through Jesus Christ.
Maybe the people you wanted to love you never gave you the answer you hoped for.
Maybe some relationships remain painfully unfinished.
Maybe there are wounds you still bring before God.
But your story does not have to end where somebody else's rejection began.
Bring your grief to Jesus.
Bring your sins to Jesus.
Bring your exhausted striving to Jesus.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
And let His grace begin rewriting the parts of your life you thought could never change.

Leah kept saying, “Maybe this time he will love me.” But the greatest hope of her story was never the love she could persuade Jacob to give—it was the Savior God would bring into the world through her family.
